result.reason: The passage describes the school of Rabbi Yannai borrowing shevi'it produce from the poor and repaying in the eighth year, which is precisely the illustrative case described in the 'Oranges Story' section's prose.

Both items are the baraita itself and the immediate Talmudic challenge to its two cases, which together constitute the 'Braisa Setup' section's content — the baraita statement plus the gemara's questions about its obvious/incoherent cases — rather than the 'Logical Challenge' section which describes only the challenges without the baraita introduction.

The passage describes the Gemara's reinterpretation of the baraita as meaning payment and act were separated in time (not simultaneous), which directly matches the 'Resolution' section's prose about reinterpreting the braisa to mean they did not happen simultaneously.

All 8 items deal with the scenario of payment-before-intercourse and whether prior sacrifice or consecration of the payment prevents etnan status — exactly the content described in the 'Sanctification Q' prose, including Rabbi Eliezer's ruling, the Gemara's analysis of 'acquire from now' vs. not, Rav Hoshaya's dilemma about hikdish vs. hikriv, and the teiku conclusion.

The passage presents the direct contradiction between two baraitot — one permitting and one forbidding payment given after intercourse — which matches exactly the 'Contradiction' section's prose describing this very contradiction.
The passage is Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak's resolution distinguishing 'this specific lamb' from 'a lamb generally,' which is precisely what heading 0's prose describes.

The passage directly discusses the meshichah problem and its resolution via a non-Jewish prostitute (who acquires by money) and the kinyan chatzer alternative, which is exactly what the 'Non-Jewish Prostitute' prose section describes.

The passage directly discusses the apotiki (designated lien) arrangement where a man tells a woman to take the animal as payment if he fails to bring money by a certain date, which is precisely what the 'Apoteke Lien' section's prose describes and analyzes.

The passage is Rav Sheshet's objection itself — the baraita about donkey-drivers and laborers eating with a dinar — which is precisely what candidate 0 ('Rav Sheshet Q') describes as its content, while candidate 1 ('Prohibited Foods') discusses the three categories of concern and the ruling eino hoshesh, which is the follow-up analysis of the ruling rather than the objection itself.
The passage is precisely about the case where the employer says 'go eat/drink and I will reimburse you,' which is the exact scenario described in candidate 3's prose ('I Will Pay').

All four items directly discuss Rav Ḥisda's distinction about the credit-giving storekeeper (*chanvani ha-makifo*) and the gemara's internal challenge to that framework, which is precisely what the 'Chisda's View' prose describes.

The passage presents the challenge ('ve-ode') questioning whether even a storekeeper without a running tab creates an obligation, which is exactly what the prose under 'No Tab' describes as the sharp question that challenges Rav Chisda's framework, not Raba's resolution itself.

The passage contains Rava's actual statement rejecting the distinction between credit and non-credit cases, which directly corresponds to heading 0 ('Raba's Resolution') where the prose describes Rava rejecting Rav Chisda's distinction and ruling that the employer always owes the storekeeper regardless of the credit relationship.

Both items deal with the textual reconciliation of the baraita's language (*va-ani pore'ah* vs. *va-ani mchashev*) in light of the pre-payment explanation, which is precisely what candidate 1's prose describes — including Rav Zevid's objection and the proposed emendation to *va-ani mchashev*.

The passage directly illustrates Rav Ashi's explanation of the braisa as referring to the employer physically handing food to workers (natal ve-natan be-yad) and the subsequent textual emendation discussion (telu ve-ichlu), which is precisely what the 'Text Reconciliation' prose describes.

The passage presents exactly the dilemma described in 'Breaking Q' — hiring someone to break yayin nesech barrels and whether that constitutes forbidden wage — matching the prose description of that section precisely.
